articles.title: Homeowners welcome visitors to showcase greener energy
articles.summary: Visitors can speak to Dorset homeowners and see their green energy installations.
articles.body:
Dozens of households will be opening their homes to showcase their renewable energy installations and sustainable ways of living.

Members of the public can visit more than 50 properties across Dorset to see everything from solar panels to rainwater harvesting and ask the owners questions about how they made their homes more efficient.

Among those taking part is Alan Muncaster, who bought his Weymouth bungalow in 2010 and has been improving it ever since.

He said he had already recouped the money he spent on solar panels and, this year, broke even on his energy bills after selling excess electricity back to the grid.

When Muncaster moved into his two-bedroom home, it was heated by gas and had hardly any insulation.

It now has an EPC rating of A - the highest possible energy efficiency rating.

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent's Dorset Breakfast show, he said: "It was a very basic UK house. It was cold, we had damp, we had poor air quality.

"We put in whole-house ventilation with heat recovery, insulation, solar panels.

"In 2021, we put the second set of solar panels on and our first house battery.

"In 2024, we had the whole of the outside of the bungalow insulated, and installed the air source heat pump, at which point we disconnected from gas."

Visitors to the participating homes will also be able to learn how to make low-cost changes to cut energy use, reduce waste and save money, as well as looking after nature in gardens.

Muncaster said: "When we started this 16 years ago, there was nobody you could talk to or employ to tell you what to do, so I've done a lot of research."

The Greener Homes event, run by Dorset Climate Action Network (DCAN), runs over two weekends, on 17-18 and 24-25 October.

Further information can be found on the DCAN website .

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader and leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday condemned the five-day judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. He said that waving the national flag during a peaceful protest is not a crime."Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice. Students. Youth. Journalists. The INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights. Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it," Rahul Gandhi said in a post on X.AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal also criticised the arrest, questioning the detention of the CJP leaders. “Is waving our own flag in our own country a crime? This is absolutely ridiculous,” he said in a post on X.Das and Ranka were sent to five-day judicial custody and lodged in Tihar Jail on Wednesday for allegedly violating their peace bonds and trespassing into Jantar Mantar, which was recently de-notified as a designated protest site, police sources said. Bail bond formalities for their associate Ajinkya Shinde were being finalised, they added.The three CJP leaders were produced before an Executive Magistrate on Wednesday morning.Earlier on Tuesday the three leaders had been detained after breaching Jantar Mantar barricades and entering the protest site without authorisation while raising slogans demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.Police registered a case against the activists on charges including trespassing, violating prohibitory orders, breaching a peace bond and obstructing a public servant from discharging official duties, sources said. Their fault? Unfurling the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar.""Show some guts, @narendramodi. articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday accused Russia of violating a ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump after overnight Russian strikes targeted energy and critical infrastructure across Ukraine, leaving at least 600,000 people without power.Russian forces also targeted facilities belonging to Ukraine's state railway in a massive overnight attack, the railway's CEO said as cited by news agency Reuters. articles.body: Google has announced an overhaul of the Google Pay rewards programme for its Flex co-branded credit card, introduced in partnership with Axis Bank and SBI Card, as it looks to attract more users ahead of the festive shopping season. Non-Google One members will receive 1.6% back in Stars on all eligible spending after crossing the same ₹15,000 threshold.Additional savings for Google One subscribersGoogle is also introducing category-specific bonuses for Google One members.Eligible users will receive an additional 5% reward on up to Rs 5,000 spent across leading food and grocery applications during each reward cycle. articles.body: MANSA: Bulldozers rolled in and demolished the house of the main accused in the killing of anti-drug activist Parwinder Singh Jhota in Punjab’s Mansa on Wednesday.The move came after Ashwani Kumar, a medical store owner accused of shooting Jhota dead, was arrested in Salasar, Rajasthan. Kumar had fled after the shooting on Tuesday morning, prompting police teams to launch a search for him.His cousin Vipin had been arrested earlier.Jhota was shot dead on Tuesday following an altercation with Kumar over the sale of banned medicines, according to reports.Mansa SSP Vaibhav Choudhary said police personnel were deployed to maintain law and order as the administration carried out the action. He said the police had received prior intimation about the demolition and that the action was linked to alleged illegal construction.“We are here to maintain law and order. Action is being taken by the administration here. So, we had received an intimation regarding the same. So, we have come here with the force to maintain law and order. There was input regarding illegal construction and action is being taken in connection with that,” Choudhary said.The killing had triggered protests in Mansa, with protesters announcing that they would not perform Jhota’s last rites until justice was delivered and the main accused were arrested.Protesters had also called for a Punjab bandh on October 15 to protest the killing.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chandigarh | Silver Rate in Chandigarh | Bank Holidays in Chandigarh | Public Holidays in Chandigarh | Chandigarh AQI | Weather in Chandigarh | Petrol Price in Chandigarh | Diesel Price in Chandigarh | CNG Price in Chandigarh | LPG Price in ChandigarhStay updated with the latest Chandigarh news. articles.title: Parineeti Chopra questions why mothers are treated as the default parent, says fathers must share childcare duties and challenge traditional expectations
articles.summary: Actor Parineeti Chopra has raised an important question about parenting expectations: why are mothers often expected to reorganise their entire lives
articles.body: Actor Parineeti Chopra has raised an important question about parenting expectations: why are mothers often expected to reorganise their entire lives after having a child, while fathers are allowed to carry on as before? The actor, who welcomed her son with politician and husband Raghav Chadha in October 2025, has spoken about the need for both parents to take equal responsibility for raising a child.In an interview with Gulf News, Parineeti challenged the idea that a mother should automatically become the primary caregiver. She explained that she and Raghav do not believe parenting should fall predominantly on one person, arguing that a child's upbringing is a shared responsibility rather than a role assigned mainly to the mother. Her comments bring attention to a familiar debate in many households, where mothers are expected to balance childcare, household responsibilities and professional commitments, while fathers may face fewer expectations to make similar adjustments.‘Why is the mother the default parent?’Parineeti questioned why society continues to place the greater burden of parenting on mothers, even when both parents are equally responsible for bringing up a child. “The majority of this world thinks that the mother is the default parent and the only parent or the one that has to make all the changes in her life, as if the father had nothing to do with this child,” she said.The actor pointed out that although both parents are involved in a child's life, the practical expectations placed on them can be very different. Mothers are often expected to adjust their routines, careers and personal priorities around their children, while fathers may be viewed as secondary caregivers. “The child is 50-50 between the parents, right? But somehow, in our society, we have normalised just the mother doing all of it. And all the changes that must happen after a baby happen only to the mother, and the father becomes the visiting parent,” she added.Her remarks challenge the assumption that a mother should naturally take charge of most childcare duties simply because she gave birth. Instead, Parineeti believes that parenting expectations need to change so both partners are actively involved in the child's everyday life.Why fathers must step up after a baby's arrivalParineeti acknowledged that pregnancy, childbirth, feeding and postpartum recovery place physical demands on mothers that fathers do not experience in the same way. However, she stressed that this difference should not become a reason for fathers to remain less involved in raising their children. “A father biologically may be behind in the motherhood process because he is not doing the pregnancy and then feeding and the postpartum, but he is very much the soldier behind all,” she said.Her observation highlights the distinction between the physical experience of motherhood and the shared responsibilities that follow a child's birth. While mothers may need time to recover from childbirth and adjust to the demands of caring for a newborn, fathers can support them by taking an active role in childcare and family life. This involvement, according to Parineeti's broader argument, should not be limited to helping when asked. Fathers are also parents and should be expected to participate in the daily responsibilities of bringing up a child.‘Parenthood has to be what works for that couple’The actor also emphasised that there is no single formula that every family must follow. What matters, she suggested, is that couples decide how to manage parenting based on their circumstances rather than allowing social expectations to dictate their roles. “I just hope that at least effort-wise and intention-wise the roles are not tipped only in favour of the mother taking over everything. Parenthood has to be what works for that couple, and society cannot dictate,” Parineeti said.Her comments underline the importance of communication and mutual support between partners. Families may divide responsibilities differently depending on work schedules, personal circumstances and the needs of the child. However, that arrangement should be a conscious decision between the parents, rather than an expectation that the mother will automatically shoulder most of the burden.Parineeti's return to work after becoming a motherParineeti and Raghav welcomed their son, Neer, in October 2025. During her pregnancy, the actor took time away from work as she prepared for motherhood and adjusted to the demands of a major change in her personal life. She has since returned to acting with two OTT releases, Shaq: Trust No One and Reporting Live, marking her comeback after a break from the screen.Her recent comments also draw attention to the challenges working mothers can face when balancing professional ambitions with the expectations surrounding childcare. Taking time off during pregnancy and returning to work after childbirth can involve significant adjustments, but Parineeti's argument is that these changes should not be treated as the mother's responsibility alone. By questioning why mothers are automatically considered the default parents, the actor has called for a more balanced approach to raising children, one in which fathers are recognised as equally responsible caregivers and couples are free to decide what works best for their families.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Constitution, not convenience’: Harvard-affiliated Indians hit out at anti-EC protests
articles.summary: A group of Indian citizens affiliated with Harvard University has raised concerns over what it described as a “concerted campaign” against the country's
articles.body: A group of Indian citizens affiliated with Harvard University has raised concerns over what it described as a “concerted campaign” against the country's constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission, the Supreme Court, the office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Parliament.In a statement issued on Wednesday, the signatories also flagged reports of Harvard University's name being used to lend credibility to a political campaign without appropriate authorisation, while calling for greater respect for constitutional values and democratic institutions."We are deeply concerned by the negative public discourse and concerted campaign against India’s constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission of India, the Supreme Court, the office of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and Parliament," the statement said.The signatories expressed concern over public discourse surrounding constitutional authorities, particularly the use of terms such as “thieves” and “compromised” to describe them, and references to India being under “siege”.Such language, they said, raised serious concerns about attempts to undermine public trust in democratic institutions.“The language used to describe India as being under ‘siege’ and to characterise constitutional authorities as ‘thieves’ or ‘compromised’ raises serious concerns about the intent to undermine public trust in democratic institutions,” the statement read.‘Evidence, not accusations’The statement also addressed the role of law enforcement agencies in maintaining public order, saying their actions should be subject to fair scrutiny but that allegations must be grounded in evidence and due process.“The actions of law enforcement agencies to uphold public order deserve fair scrutiny, but sweeping accusations and abusive rhetoric cannot substitute for evidence, due process or institutional accountability,” the signatories said.They also stressed the need to respect public officials and the offices they hold, adding that constitutional principles and civil liberties must not be applied selectively.“The Constitution, rule of law, and civil liberties must be respected at all times, not just when it suits our interests,” the statement said.Summing up their appeal, the signatories said: “Our commitment must remain to the Constitution, not convenience; to justice, not selective outrage; and to democratic institutions, not the politics of accusation.”The signatories listed affiliations with several Harvard schools, including Harvard Medical School, Harvard Kennedy School, Harvard Law School, Harvard Business School, Harvard Extension School, Harvard Divinity School, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Graduate School of Education.Among those named were AK Raghawan and Abhigyan Satyam of Harvard Medical School; Abhishek M, Banu Nagarajan, Bhavya Bishnoi, Deepanshu Aggarwal, Divya Dwivedi and Jaya Awasthi of Harvard Kennedy School; and Adhitya Srinivasan and Almas Lokhandwala of Harvard Law School.The statement comes as opposition parties and the Cockroach Janta Party have been protesting against the alleged irregularities in the special intensive revision (SIR) of voter rolls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Ohio family farmed the same land for at least three generations; then a pipeline linked to Meta’s data center was mapped across 40 acres, but after the family challenged it, the developer chose another route
articles.summary: For at least three generations, the Luidhardt family has farmed land north of Bowling Green, Ohio.
articles.body: For at least three generations, the Luidhardt family has farmed land north of Bowling Green, Ohio. That continuity came under pressure when the family learned that a natural gas pipeline connected to Meta’s data centre in Middleton Township could cross roughly 40 acres of their soybean fields. After Jon and Ken Luidhardt challenged the proposed route through the Ohio Power Siting Board, the developer ultimately selected a different path, according to BG Independent News and The Cool Down.The dispute became a broader test of how farmland, family heritage, and private corporate development collide in the age of rapid data-centre expansion. While Williams, the pipeline company’s parent firm, says it never pursued or threatened eminent domain on the route submitted for review, the Luidhardts say a map showed the pipeline crossing their property and that they felt compelled to fight back.A farm with deep family rootsJon Luidhardt said the land has been in his family for at least three generations, and he wants future generations to continue farming it. “We want to continue a fourth and fifth generation of farming,” he told BG Independent News.The property lies near the corner of Haskins Road and Hannah Road, between Bowling Green and Haskins. Its value to the family was not only agricultural, but also personal, because it represented continuity, work, and a way of life passed down over decades.That history helps explain why the family rejected a financial offer to sell part of the acreage. Luidhardt said pipeline representatives offered what he described as an “insane amount of money,” with some offers reportedly reaching as much as $200,000 per acre, but he argued that money could not replace family history.A pipeline for Meta’s data centerWill-Power, a pipeline company connected to Williams, sought land for a natural gas pipeline intended to serve the Meta data centre being built in Middleton Township. The pipeline would support the Apollo power plant, a natural gas facility located east of the data centre. The Apollo plant was approved by the Ohio Power Siting Board in February under an expedited review process. It will operate “behind the meter,” meaning it will serve the electricity needs of the adjacent Meta data centre rather than being physically connected to the public power grid, as per the reports.Because the facility is dedicated to a single customer, the approval process did not include public hearings. That lack of broader public involvement became a central concern for opponents, who argued that the project was designed to benefit one private company rather than the wider community.The family’s legal challengeThe reports further suggested that when Jon Luidhardt saw a map indicating that the pipeline would cross the family’s soybean field, he and his father contacted attorney Maurice Thompson, executive director of the 1851 Center for Constitutional Law in Columbus. The family had previously worked with Thompson to stop another pipeline from crossing their land. Thompson filed a motion to intervene with the Ohio Power Siting Board. He argued that private property in Ohio should not be taken simply to benefit a purely private corporate project, including a private pipeline built to fuel that project.The legal argument focused on eminent domain, the government power to take private property for public use. Thompson contended that the Apollo pipeline was solely intended to fuel Meta, rather than to heat Ohio homes or fuel vehicles, and therefore did not meet the traditional public-use standard.The developer says it chose another routeAfter the family’s challenge, Thompson said Will-Power informed regulators that the line would be redirected around Luidhardt Farms and removed from the family’s property. However, at the time of publication, the Luidhardts had not yet seen the revised map. Williams disputed the characterisation that eminent domain had been used or threatened. A company representative said the Luidhardt property was not on the route submitted for review and that the company had already achieved 100 percent acquisition before the farmer filed the intervention.The representative also said that all land options for the project involved voluntary agreements and that Williams did not pursue or threaten eminent domain against any landowner affected by the route. The company has previously described eminent domain as a last resort for pipeline projects.Why the case mattersThe dispute raises questions about whether state authority should be used to help a private corporation secure land for infrastructure that mainly benefits its own operations. Thompson argued that eminent domain is generally meant to serve a public use, not the needs of one private business.The case also reflects a wider tension between data-centre growth and rural communities. As companies build large facilities that require substantial electricity, water, and fuel infrastructure, nearby landowners may face pressure to sell or alter land that has been farmed for generations.There are environmental concerns as well. The pipeline would support a natural gas-powered facility for the data centre, potentially locking in additional polluting infrastructure as communities weigh the costs of rapid industrial expansion.What happens nextFor the Luidhardts, the reported reroute offers reassurance, but it does not fully close the issue. Jon Luidhardt said he wants to see the updated filing before treating the matter as resolved, and he also wanted the case tested in court.Thompson’s intervention did not produce a court ruling, but it appears to have contributed to the company’s decision to pursue a different route. He argued that public scrutiny can change corporate behaviour, saying that when the issue is highlighted, companies often find another way forward.The outcome is a partial victory for the family, but it also illustrates the uncertainty many landowners face when major infrastructure projects approach their property. A pipeline route can shift, offers can be substantial, and legal challenges may not always result in a formal ruling, yet they can still influence the final decision.A question of land, power, and progressThe Luidhardt case is ultimately about more than one pipeline or one data centre. It asks whether long-standing family farms should be preserved when a private development promises economic growth but requires land that families have cultivated for generations.Meta and its pipeline affiliates remain free to buy land from willing sellers. The dispute centred on whether a project serving a single private company should be able to rely on the power of eminent domain, or the threat of it, to overcome a landowner’s refusal.For now, the Luidhardt family’s land appears to be off the route. Their challenge shows how local opposition, legal intervention, and public attention can shape decisions about where large-scale infrastructure is placed, even in an era when data centres are expanding rapidly across the United States.You use AI every day.
